title: Storyboard: Talking Bedrock with customers
intro: The storyboard is the design record behind the module: who it is for, what a learner can do afterward, what appears on each screen, and how each part is measured. It matches the build scene for scene.
audience: Inside sales representatives and sales leaders who are new to generative AI and need to hold a credible first conversation about Amazon Bedrock with customers, from startup founders to C-suite executives.
goal: After the module, a rep can open a conversation by finding a use case, place it in one of three adoption zones, frame a model-selection discussion with seven criteria, and stay honest and useful when capacity is limited.
approach: Action mapping: begin with the on-the-job behavior and keep only the content that supports it.
Scenario-based practice: three branching customer conversations with a strong, a partial, and a weak answer at each decision, and feedback that explains why.
Stable framework, swappable reference: product details change quickly, so the seven criteria stay put and facts live in one content file with a verify-before-quoting note.

Learner control with guardrails: a contents list and a progress bar show where the learner is and let them return to any step they have unlocked. Continue stays locked until a step's activities are done, so the assessment cannot be skipped.

Accessible by default: keyboard operable, focus kept in place after each choice, screen reader announcements and labeled tabs and progress, color never the only signal, large touch targets, works at phone width, respects reduced motion.

scenes.title: Welcome
scenes.objective: Set expectations and show what the learner will be able to do.
scenes.onScreen: Title, a one-sentence promise, an illustration of the central exchange (the customer asks where to start; the seller asks about their work), four performance objectives, a plain summary of how the module is scored, how to move around, and a note that Bedrock facts change and should be verified before quoting to customers.
scenes.interaction: None. Learners can resume where they left off or start over.
scenes.assessment: None. The scoring summary is here so learners know what counts before they make a single decision.
scenes.rationale: Objectives are written as behaviors the learner can do on a call, not topics they will see. Saying up front how scoring works removes guesswork.

scenes.title: The real question
scenes.objective: Feel the difference between pitching a product and finding a use case.
scenes.onScreen: A CEO says: "Our investors keep asking about our AI plan. Where do we even start?" Three possible replies.
scenes.interaction: Choose one reply. The choice locks and feedback appears.
scenes.feedback: Each reply explains why it works or doesn't. The strong reply asks about a process or customer moment.
scenes.assessment: Unscored. It sets up the rest of the module.
scenes.rationale: The line mirrors what executives said under investor pressure. Starting with it makes the learner's first decision the central skill.

scenes.title: Three zones
scenes.objective: Place a customer's use case in back office, middle office, or customer-facing, and know the first question for each.
scenes.onScreen: Tabs for each zone with who it covers, examples, what to watch for, and the first question to ask. Then three customer statements to sort.
scenes.interaction: Browse the tabs, then sort three statements into zones.
scenes.feedback: Immediate, with a one-line reason for each statement.
scenes.assessment: Unscored practice. Reinforced in the knowledge check.
scenes.rationale: New sellers don't need an AI taxonomy. They need a quick way to decide what to ask next. Three zones is small enough to remember on a call.

scenes.title: Choosing a model family
scenes.objective: Use seven criteria to frame a model-selection discussion without claiming to pick the model.
scenes.onScreen: Seven expandable criteria, each with a plain-language meaning and a question to ask. Then a four-question planner that returns a talk track.
scenes.interaction: Open criteria at will. Answer four questions about an imaginary customer to see a talk track.
scenes.feedback: The planner output changes with the answers and always ends with: the model choice is a test result, not a sales claim.
scenes.assessment: Unscored. The final line is tested in the knowledge check.
scenes.rationale: Sellers frame the conversation and bring in a solutions architect for the comparison. The planner models that division of labor and avoids model names that would go stale.

scenes.title: Conversation 1: the technical founder
scenes.objective: Diagnose a technical buyer's workload before pitching, and route depth questions to a specialist.
scenes.onScreen: A startup CTO asks why she should move to Bedrock. Two decisions, three replies each.
scenes.interaction: Choose a reply at each decision. The second decision depends on the conversation, not on the first choice.
scenes.feedback: Strong, partly right, or weak, with a reason, then a short takeaway.
scenes.rationale: Feature tours lose technical buyers. The scenario rewards questions about cost, speed, quality, and security reviews.

scenes.title: Conversation 2: the executive under investor pressure
scenes.objective: Offer a small, measurable first step and an honest account of cost.
scenes.onScreen: A COO owned by a private equity firm wants an AI plan without a science project. Two decisions.
scenes.feedback: Same structure. Weak answers include fear-based urgency and unsupported savings claims.
scenes.rationale: This is the conversation the case is named for. The strong path defines success first, then proves it in a pilot.

scenes.title: Conversation 3: the capacity-constrained launch
scenes.objective: Stay credible when supply is limited: no promises, gather the load facts, use the escalation path, set a check-in date.
scenes.onScreen: A VP of Engineering hit throughput limits and asks for a capacity guarantee four weeks before launch. Two decisions.
scenes.feedback: Weak answers promise or predict availability. Strong answers are honest, specific, and give a next date.
scenes.rationale: Capacity was a real constraint in 2024 and 2025. Treating it as a conversation skill keeps the content useful and avoids internal allocation detail.

scenes.title: Knowledge check
scenes.objective: Confirm the learner can apply the core ideas.
scenes.onScreen: Five multiple-choice questions on opening move, zones, selection criteria, capacity conversations, and who decides the model.
scenes.interaction: Choose one answer per question. Answers lock with immediate feedback.
scenes.feedback: A one-sentence explanation for every question.
scenes.assessment: 1 point each, 5 points. Together with the scenarios, 17 points. Pass mark 80%.
scenes.rationale: Questions test decisions, not recall of product facts.

scenes.title: Results and job aid
scenes.objective: Report the outcome and leave the learner with something to use on the next call.
scenes.onScreen: Score, pass or retry, a points breakdown, and a one-page job aid: three first questions, seven criteria, a capacity checklist, and the closing rule.
scenes.interaction: Retry the conversations and quiz if under the pass mark. Print the job aid.
scenes.assessment: Reports score and pass or fail to the LMS (SCORM 1.2) when launched from one.
scenes.rationale: The job aid is the part reps will actually reuse. It prints cleanly on one page.

measurement.question: Did reps find it useful and credible?
Can reps make good decisions in the conversations?
measurement.measure: Scenario points and knowledge check score (SCORM score)

measurement.question: Are reps creating Bedrock opportunities?
measurement.measure: New Bedrock opportunities per rep per month
measurement.source: Reported: 1 to 2 per rep per month across about 50 reps, up from 0

measurement.question: Did Bedrock pipeline move?
measurement.source: Reported: 3% confirm what it is a percentage of
